newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Inchcape sells Bain Hogg, wipes debt.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Inchcape sells Bain Hogg, wipes debt.

text.p: Struggling international trading group Inchcape said on Tuesday it had sold its insurance broking arm Bain Hogg to U.S. broking giant Aon Corp, completing a plan designed to clear hundreds of millions of pounds in debts and refocus the group more on its core distribution businesses.

Aon, the second biggest insurance broker in the world, is to pay 160 million pounds ($253 million) for Bain Hogg, which has a significant share of the hard pressed British retail insurance market, where premiums have been falling and growth is elusive.
Inchcape said only three weeks ago it would probably demerge Bain Hogg in order to reduce group borrowings.
But on Tuesday it said it believed the sale price to Aon represented better value than demerger. However, some analysts wondered if Bain Hogg was not worth more.

Aon is likely to integrate Bain Hogg with its other British insurance broking interests, wholesale reinsurance specialist Nicholson Jenner Leslie and Aon Risk Services, a much smaller retail broking operation, industry sources said.

This should result in substantial cost savings. Staff numbers in the combined operation would probably be cut. Bain Hogg employs 4,500 people worldwide, while Aon's UK activities have a 3,000 strong workforce, the industry sources said.
"This acquisition augments our global leadership position in insurance services and distribution," Patrick Ryan, chairman and chief executive of Aon Corp, said in a statement.
"We continue to look for other quality brokerage opportunities where shared culture and sound financial principles for valuing brokerage businesses will permit us to deploy our assets," he added.
Inchcape will shoulder an exceptional loss of about 195 million pounds from the sale.
Analysts say the value of Bain Hogg at demerger would have been 130 million pounds, while Inchcape would have needed to plough in 13 million to give it sufficient capital.
Restructuring costs would be another 20 million pounds.
Chief executive Philip Cushing said several buyers including other brokers approached had Inchcape about Bain Hogg after the parent announced in March that the divestment was planned.
"We've said consistently we were going to exit this year and (last month) we said that the most probable route was demerger and that may have focused people's minds," he told Reuters.
Together with the disposal in September of its quality testing unit for 380 million pounds, Inchcape's twin divestment plan has suceeded in cutting group debt to minimal levels.
But it has also diluted earnings as both businesses are more profitable than its core auto and consumer product distribution, marketing and bottling activities.

Borrowings at the end of 1995 stood at a net level of 463 million pounds. The effect of the two transactions would be to reduce the gearing of 74 percent at this year's six month point to just five percent on a proforma basis, the company said.
"Now we can get on with our business as an international distributor pure and simple for the future," Cushing said.

Some analysts wondered if Bain Hogg had not been disposed of too cheaply, especially as last year, both it and U.S. rival Alexander & Alexander tabled bids for the company pitched just over 160 million pounds.
However, Inchcape has made clear that Bain Hogg has had a poor year so far, with pretax profits slipping in the first half to 20.1 million pounds from 24.9 million a year ago.
By contrast Bain Hogg's bigger UK rival Sedgwick, which had been tipped as a possible target for Aon, saw interim profits edge up to 64.1 million pounds from 63.1 million.
